title: Candy
directAnswer: Each child needs ≥ 1 candy, and a child with a higher rating than a neighbor must get more than that neighbor. The clean answer is two greedy passes: left-to-right enforce the 'greater than left neighbor' rule, then right-to-left enforce 'greater than right neighbor' while taking the max of the two demands. Summing the per-child maxima gives the minimum total. O(n) time, O(n) space (an O(1)-space one-pass exists).

remember.pattern: Two greedy sweeps (left→right, right→left, take max)
rules: Start everyone at **1** — that satisfies the 'at least one candy' floor.
Left pass fixes the **left-neighbor** constraint; right pass fixes the **right-neighbor** constraint.
On the right pass, **take the max** — never overwrite the left pass's result, or you break one side.
**Equal ratings impose no constraint** — neighbors with the same rating may differ freely in candy.
One constraint per direction means one pass per direction; a single pass can't see both neighbors at once.
whenToUse: Assign values under local neighbor constraints in both directions
Minimize a total subject to 'strictly greater than smaller neighbor'
Any 1-D problem where each element depends on left AND right context
antiSignals: Constraint is only one-directional → a single pass suffices
Constraint is non-local (depends on all elements) → not a sweep; think DP or sorting
You need the assignment to be unique → this yields the minimum, not the only valid one
Ratings form a 2-D grid → BFS/DP by value order, not a linear sweep
remember.takeaway: Two-directional local constraints split into two one-directional sweeps whose results you combine with max. Candy is the archetype: decompose a 'both neighbors' rule into a left pass and a right pass, then reconcile. The same decomposition powers Trapping Rain Water and Product of Array Except Self.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize that a both-neighbors constraint decomposes into two independent one-directional passes, and whether you correctly combine them with max instead of overwriting.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Trying to solve it in a single pass (you can't satisfy both neighbors at once), or overwriting instead of taking max on the right pass — which breaks the left-neighbor guarantee.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the decomposition explicitly (left rule, right rule, reconcile with max), prove minimality, and offer the O(1)-space one-pass slope-counting solution as the follow-up.

problemStatement:
There are `n` children standing in a line, each assigned a rating value given in the integer array `ratings`.

You are giving candies to these children subject to the following requirements:

- Each child must have **at least one** candy.
- Children with a higher rating get **more** candies than their neighbors.

Return the **minimum** number of candies you need to have to distribute the candies to the children.
understanding: Give each child at least one candy, and strictly more than any adjacent child with a lower rating — in BOTH directions. Equal-rated neighbors have no relationship. Minimize the total. The constraint couples each child to its left and right neighbor, which is why one sweep can't do it.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the 'more than neighbors' rule apply to both the left and right neighbor?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — a child with a higher rating than EITHER neighbor must out-candy that neighbor. That two-sided coupling is exactly why we need two passes.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What happens when two adjacent children have equal ratings?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No constraint between them. They can have any candy counts (each still ≥ 1). This is the detail that keeps it from being a strict monotonic assignment.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I need to return the assignment or just the total?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just the minimum total count. The per-child assignment is computed internally but only the sum is returned.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is there always a valid distribution?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — giving everyone 1 already satisfies the floor, and the passes only ever increase counts, so a valid (and minimal) solution always exists.

examples.explanation: Candies [2,1,2]: child 0 (rating 1) > child 1 (rating 0); child 2 (rating 2) > child 1. Total 5.
Candies [1,2,1]: child 1 > child 0. Children 1 and 2 are equal-rated, so no constraint — child 2 can drop back to 1. Total 4.
Candies [1,2,1,2,1]: the peak at index 1 beats its left; the descent 2,2,1 is handled by the right pass. Total 7.

diagrams.title: Decomposing the two-sided constraint
diagrams.caption: One pass per direction, reconciled by max. The two-pass greedy is the standard answer.

approaches.name: Two Passes (Left→Right then Right→Left)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Lead with the decomposition insight: a both-neighbors rule = a left rule + a right rule, reconciled with max.
hints: A child must beat BOTH neighbors when it's rated higher. Can one left-to-right pass ever know about the neighbor to its right? What does that suggest about how many passes you need?
Pass 1 (left→right): give everyone 1, then whenever ratings[i] > ratings[i-1], set candy[i] = candy[i-1] + 1. This satisfies every left-neighbor constraint.
Pass 2 (right→left): whenever ratings[i] > ratings[i+1], set candy[i] = max(candy[i], candy[i+1] + 1). The max preserves pass 1's work while adding the right-neighbor guarantee.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Two linear passes → O(n) time. A candy[] array of size n → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
The constraint 'a higher-rated child gets more candy than its neighbors' is *two-sided*: it talks about the left neighbor and the right neighbor simultaneously. A single left-to-right scan structurally cannot satisfy it, because when you assign `candy[i]` you haven't yet seen `candy[i+1]`. The key insight is to **split the two-sided rule into two one-sided rules** and handle each with its own directional pass.

**Pass 1 — satisfy the left neighbor.** Initialize every child to `1` (the floor). Sweep left to right; whenever `ratings[i] > ratings[i-1]`, the current child outranks the one on its left, so it must have strictly more: set `candy[i] = candy[i-1] + 1`. After this pass, *every* 'greater than left neighbor' constraint holds, and ascending runs get the staircase `1,2,3,…` they require. What's *not* yet handled: a child that should beat its *right* neighbor (the descending side of a peak).

**Pass 2 — satisfy the right neighbor, without breaking pass 1.** Sweep right to left; whenever `ratings[i] > ratings[i+1]`, the child must out-candy its right neighbor, demanding at least `candy[i+1] + 1`. Here is the crucial move: we write **`candy[i] = max(candy[i], candy[i+1] + 1)`**, not a plain assignment. The `max` is what makes the two passes compose. `candy[i]` already encodes the left-neighbor requirement from pass 1; the right pass only *raises* it if the right-neighbor requirement is stronger. Overwriting instead would discard the left guarantee and produce an invalid distribution at peaks that tower over both sides.

**Why the result is minimal.** Every increment we perform is *forced*: we only ever bump a child to exactly one more than the neighbor that forces it, and we take the smaller value that still satisfies both sides (`max` of two tight lower bounds is itself the tight lower bound). No child is ever larger than it must be, so the sum is the minimum. A child sitting at a peak ends up at `max(leftRun, rightRun) + 1`, which is precisely the smallest value exceeding both descending/ascending slopes — exactly right.

**Why equal ratings need no special handling.** When `ratings[i] == ratings[i-1]`, neither `>` test fires, so neither pass raises the child on account of that neighbor. It stays at whatever the other side demands (often back down to `1`), which is why `[1,2,2]` correctly yields `[1,2,1]` rather than forcing the second `2` upward.
approaches.insight: A constraint that references both neighbors decomposes into two independent single-direction constraints. Solve each with a directional sweep, then reconcile per element with max. The max is the linchpin — it lets the second pass strengthen the first without erasing it.

pitfalls: Overwriting instead of max on the right pass — destroys the left-neighbor guarantee at peaks.
Using >= instead of > — equal ratings impose no constraint; >= over-allocates.
Doing only one pass — leaves every right-side descent under-allocated.

approaches.name: One Pass, O(1) Space (Slope Counting)
approaches.whenToMention: Offer when asked to remove the O(n) array. It tracks ascending/descending run lengths instead of storing per-child candy. Harder to get right — only attempt it if you can explain the peak adjustment.
hints: You don't actually need the whole candy array — only the running length of the current ascending run and descending run.
On an increase, extend the up-run and add its new length. On a decrease, extend the down-run and add its length.
The peak between an up-run and a down-run is shared; when the down-run hasn't yet exceeded the up-run's height, you've counted the peak twice and must subtract one.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single left-to-right pass with a handful of integer counters → O(n) time, O(1) extra space (no candy array).
approaches.explanation:
The two-pass method stores a candy count per child, costing `O(n)` memory. But the only thing that determines a child's candy is the length of the monotonic run it sits in. Tracking those run lengths lets us accumulate the total in one pass without the array.

**The counters.** Walk left to right maintaining `up` (length of the current strictly-increasing run), `down` (length of the current strictly-decreasing run), and `peak` (the `up` value captured at the most recent peak). Start the total at `n` — that pre-pays the floor of one candy for everyone, so each addition below represents only the *extra* candies beyond the floor.

**Rising.** When `ratings[i] > ratings[i-1]`, we're climbing: increment `up`, reset `down = 0`, and record `peak = up`. The climber needs `up` more candies than the valley it started from, so add `up` to the total. (A staircase `1,2,3` adds `0+1+2` extra over the floor — correct.)

**Falling.** When `ratings[i] < ratings[i-1]`, we're descending: increment `down`, reset `up = 0`, and add `down`. Giving the descending children `1,2,3,…` from the bottom up keeps each strictly above its right neighbor. **The subtlety:** the peak at the top of the descent is shared between the up-run and the down-run. While the descent is still shorter than or equal to the peak's height (`peak >= down`), the peak is already tall enough to dominate the descent, and our `+= down` has implicitly counted the peak once too often — so we subtract `1`. Once the descent grows *longer* than the peak (`down > peak`), the peak genuinely must be raised to stay above the lengthening descent, and the `+= down` correctly performs that raise without subtraction.

**Flat.** When ratings are equal, all runs reset to `0` and nothing is added beyond the already-counted floor — matching the 'no constraint between equals' rule.

**Why two-pass is still the better interview answer.** This one-pass version is provably equivalent and saves memory, but its correctness rests on the peak-sharing adjustment that's easy to bungle under pressure. Unless the interviewer explicitly demands `O(1)` space, present the two-pass solution (whose minimality is transparent) and mention this as the optimization you'd reach for when memory is tight.
approaches.insight: A child's candy is fully determined by the length of the monotonic run it belongs to, so you can sum the total from run-length counters alone. The only trap is the shared peak between an ascent and a descent — subtract one until the descent outgrows the ascent.

java.explanation: Pre-pay the floor of one candy per child; additions below are the extras.

java.line: up++; down = 0; peak = up; total += up;
java.explanation: Rising: extend the up-run and add its length; remember the peak height.
Equal ratings reset all runs — no constraint between equals.

java.line: down++; total += down; if (peak >= down) total--;
java.explanation: Falling: add the down length; subtract one while the peak still dominates the descent.

python.line: up += 1; down = 0; peak = up; total += up
python.explanation: Ascending step contributes its run length.
Flat segment clears the run state.

python.line: down += 1; total += down; if peak >= down: total -= 1
python.explanation: Descending step adds down; the −1 removes the double-counted shared peak.

edgeCases.behavior: All descending, peak stays 0 so no subtraction → total 5+1+2+3+4 = 15.
i=1 up=1 total→4; i=2 equal resets → total 4.

pitfalls: Forgetting to reset down (and peak) when a new ascent starts — leaks stale run lengths.
Subtracting unconditionally on every descent instead of only while peak >= down — under-counts long descents.
Not resetting runs on equal ratings — treats a flat as part of a slope.

commonMistakes: Attempting a single pass — it can't satisfy the left and right neighbor at the same time.
Overwriting candy[i] on the right pass instead of taking max — breaks the left-neighbor guarantee.
Treating equal-rated neighbors as a constraint (using >=) and over-allocating candy.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Overwriting instead of taking max on the right pass
commonMistakesDetailed.why: At a peak that beats both neighbors, the left pass already set a large value. A plain assignment on the right pass discards it, so the peak may end up ≤ its left neighbor — invalid.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Using >= and over-allocating on equal ratings
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Equal-rated neighbors have NO ordering constraint. Using >= forces a strict increase that isn't required, inflating the total (e.g. [1,2,2] would wrongly cost 5 instead of 4).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Solving it in one greedy pass
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A single left-to-right pass can't see the right neighbor, so descents after a peak get only 1 candy and violate the rule. You need a second pass (or run-length tracking) to handle the other direction.

patternNote: Two-directional local constraint solved by a left pass + a right pass reconciled with max (with an O(1) slope-counting one-pass variant). Recognise it whenever each element's value depends on both its neighbors. Same decomposition as Trapping Rain Water and Product of Array Except Self.
